limit/fixed: Gated DeltaNet keeps a state of fixed size however long the text, and that is its strength.
limit/cap: It is also its limit. With keys of d k numbers, at most d k of them can be at right angles, so only that many pairs can be held perfectly apart.
limit/share: Across a hundred thousand tokens, most pairs must share the state: the gates and the delta rule choose what to keep, and some facts are lost.
limit/drop: In the needle test with real essays, even Gated DeltaNet found the needle less than a third of the time at eight thousand tokens.
limit/cache: Softmax attention keeps every key and value in its cache, so a query can still find a token from far back, at the price of a cache that grows with the text.
limit/gap: On real tasks that look facts up in long documents, Yang's team found pure recurrent models well behind transformers, while models that mixed in some attention beat both.
mix/idea: So mix them. Keep most layers recurrent, with fixed states, and make every few layers full softmax attention, with a cache of every token.
mix/yang: In 2024, Yang's team tried it with DeltaNet: swapping just two of its layers for full attention gave a model that beat a transformer of the same size.
mix/qwen: In 2025, the Qwen team at Alibaba built a large model this way, Qwen three Next: forty eight layers, in twelve groups of three Gated DeltaNet layers and one attention layer.
mix/why: Their reason: linear attention is fast but weak at recall, and standard attention is expensive and slow when generating. Three to one did better than either kind alone.
mix/count: So only twelve of the forty eight layers keep a KV cache.
memory/full: Now the memory, for a made-up model with the same pattern: forty eight layers, d of four thousand, two bytes a number. As a transformer, it would need about seventy seven gigabytes of cache for a hundred thousand tokens.
memory/formula: That is two, for keys and values, times forty eight layers, a hundred thousand tokens, four thousand numbers each, and two bytes.
memory/hybrid: In the hybrid, only twelve layers keep a cache: a quarter of it, about nineteen gigabytes.
memory/state: The other thirty six keep states. At half a million numbers each, a megabyte, that is thirty six megabytes, at any length.
memory/grow: Double the context, and the cache doubles: it still grows in proportion to the tokens, four times slower than the transformer's. The states stay the same.
memory/trade: Fewer attention layers would shrink the cache further, but leave more of the recall to fixed states: the ratio is the trade-off.
